name: Priya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Marsh Farm, which is my partner Sam's family's place. It's mixed, about sixty beef cattle, two hundred ewes, some barley, hens, and a farm shop at the end of the drive selling our own meat, eggs and Ruth's jams. Ruth is Sam's mum. Mornings I'm feeding and checking stock with Sam, and from ten I'm in the shop, and in between I'm doing the online orders on my phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the shop on a Saturday, when it's full and people are chatting at the counter about whose lambs are out. What wears me out is that I'm the newcomer. I grew up in a flat in town, so I'm learning lambing and calving from scratch, and Geoff, Sam's dad, still checks everything I do twice. Fair enough, I got a ewe stuck in a gate last week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use technology, day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, constantly. I use AI for the shop's posts, the price labels, working out how much stock to order before a long weekend, even writing the little stories about each animal for the meat boxes. Geoff thinks it's witchcraft. Ruth's started asking me to do her emails with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's brilliant and I'd show anyone who asked. Since I started doing the online orders with AI help, our meat box sales have nearly doubled in a year. Small family businesses should be using it. That's what I'd tell the other farm shops at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still on very little. Ruth and Geoff pay me what they can, which isn't much, and Sam and I have about a month's money if that. We live in the caravan behind the barn while we save. A better tool helps the farm, but I need the farm to be able to pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push the online side harder. Start a Christmas hamper page by October. Do the lambing course at the college in February so Geoff stops checking me twice. And keep helping with the harvest supper at church, because half our customers come from there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. I like this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's it like working for your partner's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly lovely, sometimes hard. You can't really ask your future mother-in-law for a raise. I'd rather earn it by showing the numbers, and the meat boxes are the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'future mother-in-law'. Are you and Sam planning to marry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next summer, in the village church. Sam's grandad's buried in that churchyard. That's partly why I care so much about this farm working. It's not a job, it's going to be our family.

S0.say: I'd say it's brilliant and show anyone who asked, because our meat box sales nearly doubled in a year once I used AI for online orders. Small family businesses should be using it.
S0.think: Privately I'm still on very little, and Sam and I have about a month's money while we live in a caravan behind the barn. A better tool helps the farm, but the farm has to be able to pay me.
S0.do: Pushes the online shop harder, starting a Christmas hamper page by October. Takes the lambing course at the college in February and keeps helping at the church harvest supper, where many customers come from.
S0.quote: You can't really ask your future mother-in-law for a raise. I'd rather earn it by showing the numbers, and the meat boxes are the numbers.
S0.fieldNote: The most commercially minded person in this group, and a daily AI user who credits it with doubling meat box sales. Her traditional outlook shows through family, church and marrying into the farm. She's paid very little and handles that by proving her value, not asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a pity, because young people need a start. But a family farm is always a good start, if you've got family. I'd say more farms should take on young people the old way, live in, learn on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it suits us. We're not a company hiring beginners, we're a family, and I'm already in. Slow AI means I can keep adding things, the website, better records, without anything frightening happening. If anything, other farms will need someone like me to help them catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn every bit of the stock work so I'm not just the shop girl who married in. Maybe start helping two or three other farm shops set up their online orders, for a fee. Talk to Sam about whether that's a side business or a distraction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the shop girl who married in'. Is that how people see you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the old farmers at the market, yes. One of them asked Geoff if I was the new help. I laughed, but it stung. That's why I want to be good at lambing, not just the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Geoff and Ruth mind you helping other farm shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would love it, she's very proud of me. Geoff would worry I'm helping the competition. I'd say there's enough people for everyone, and our sausages are better anyway.

S1.say: I'd say it's a pity for young people, but a family farm is always a good start. More farms should take young people on the old way, living in and learning on the job.
S1.think: Honestly I think it suits us, because we're a family and I'm already in. Slow change lets me keep adding things like the website and records, and other farms will need help catching up.
S1.do: Learns every part of the stock work so she isn't seen as just the shop worker who married in. Starts helping two or three other farm shops set up online orders for a fee, after talking it through with Sam.
S1.quote: One of them asked Geoff if I was the new help. I laughed, but it stung.
S1.fieldNote: Her drive comes partly from wanting respect as a farmer, not just as the person good with phones. She sees slow AI as a business opening, not a threat. Her traditional view of farms as a start in life sits easily with her enthusiasm for technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people in offices should be helped to find new work, but not paid to sit at home. And I'd say come and buy from farm shops, support real local businesses. That's a bit of a sales pitch, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about our customers. Half our meat box buyers are office people from town, teachers, people at the council, the insurance office. If they lose jobs or take pay cuts, they stop buying big boxes of beef at full price. The shop's the thing that pays my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make cheaper boxes, sausages and mince, smaller sizes, before the sales drop. Use AI to track which customers stop ordering and send them something to bring them back. Keep a close eye on the till every week and tell Ruth straight if it's dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The farm's fine. The shop's the soft part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the shop's sales dropped by a third, what would happen at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and Geoff would cut my hours before they'd cut the farm. We'd probably delay the wedding, or make it smaller, a church and a barn instead of the hotel. Sam would say it doesn't matter. It would to me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want politicians to do anything, in all the arguing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lower taxes for small shops, so we can keep prices down. Help people get apprenticeships. I don't want big schemes. Every big scheme I've seen ends up with forms only big companies can fill in.

S2.say: I'd say office workers should be helped to find new work but not paid to sit at home. And I'd tell people to support local farm shops, which I admit is a bit of a sales pitch.
S2.think: Privately I'm worried about our customers, because half our meat box buyers are office workers from town. If they lose jobs, they stop buying big boxes of beef at full price, and the shop pays my wage.
S2.do: Brings in cheaper, smaller boxes of sausages and mince before sales drop. Uses AI to spot customers who stop ordering and win them back, and checks the till weekly with Ruth.
S2.feel: Uneasy, because the shop is the soft part of the business.
S2.quote: The farm's fine. The shop's the soft part.
S2.fieldNote: She saw immediately that office layoffs hit her through her customers, and had a pricing response ready. Her politics are small-business and anti-scheme. The wedding was the personal cost she reached for first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's never been more important, and that the people getting rich should invest in the country, in real things. Not handouts, investment. I'd also be selling to them, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mixed. Our town customers lose out, but the rich ones from the share boom will want fancy local food and weekends in the country. I could sell them hampers and farm stays. The worry is land prices. If farmland gets bought up as investments, the farm next door goes to someone who doesn't farm, and the village changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turn the empty barn into a shepherd's hut stay, a little wooden hut people rent for weekends, if Geoff agrees. Start a premium hamper line for the people doing well. Keep the cheap boxes going for the people who aren't. Save every bit we can toward a proper house on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. When I'm busy I don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell to both groups, the winners and the losers. Does that sit right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. A shop serves everyone who comes in. I'd rather the rich lot spend their money in our village than on another holiday abroad. And the cheap boxes are partly for the neighbours, so nobody's left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the church supper about the political crisis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we look after our own first, the village, the elderly, the young families. And that those who've done well should give more, out of decency, not because a politician makes them. The vicar would probably say something similar, and better.

S3.say: I'd say farming has never been more important, and the people getting rich should invest in real things in the country, not handouts. I'd also be selling to them, honestly.
S3.think: It's mixed: town customers lose out, but rich people from the share boom want local food and country weekends. My worry is land being bought as an investment by people who don't farm.
S3.do: Converts the empty barn space into a shepherd's hut for weekend stays if Geoff agrees, and launches a premium hamper line alongside cheaper boxes. Saves toward a proper house on the farm.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and being busy keeps the panic away.
S3.quote: I'd rather the rich lot spend their money in our village than on another holiday abroad.
S3.fieldNote: She splits the market cleanly into premium and budget lines, showing real business sense. Her fear sits with land prices and outside buyers changing the village. On redistribution she favours voluntary giving and local loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small family farms are where robots make least sense and people matter most. People don't drive twenty minutes for sausages. They drive for Ruth behind the counter. A robot can do the counter, but it can't be her. I'd put that on our shop page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd want one. A robot to muck out the sheds and do the night checks at lambing would give Sam and me our evenings back. But the big farms will get them first and cheaper, and they'll sell meat at prices we can't touch. That's the real threat, not the robot itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Find out what's for sale and what it really costs, then see if three or four small farms could share one, like the old machinery rings where farms shared a combine. Lean even harder on the shop and the stays, the bit that's about people. And make sure I'm the one in the family who can run the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and excited together. It's the first one where I can see us losing, but I can also see us winning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Geoff, who's suspicious of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you didn't want the website either, and look at the meat boxes. Then I'd make him a cup of tea and leave it. He comes round if you don't push him in front of other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family farms are where people matter most. Where does that leave you, the newcomer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a good question. I'm not family by blood yet, so maybe I'm the most replaceable, if I'm honest. Unless I'm the one who makes the robots work for us. Then I'm the one they can't do without.

S4.say: I'd say small family farms are where robots make least sense and people matter most. People drive for Ruth behind the counter, not for sausages, and a robot can't be her.
S4.think: Privately I'd want a robot for mucking out and night lambing checks, to give Sam and me our evenings back. The real threat is big farms getting robots first and selling meat at prices we can't match.
S4.do: Researches what robots really cost and whether three or four small farms could share one, like the old machinery-sharing groups. Puts more into the shop and farm stays, and makes herself the family member who can run the robot.
S4.feel: Anxious and excited together, able to see both losing and winning.
S4.quote: People don't drive twenty minutes for sausages. They drive for Ruth behind the counter. A robot can do the counter, but it can't be her.
S4.fieldNote: Her public line and private wish point opposite ways: she'd defend the human counter while quietly wanting a robot in the lambing shed. She admitted, when pressed, that as the newcomer she may be the most replaceable. Her answer is to become the person who makes the machines work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because the big farms win that race unless small ones stick together. What would help is grants or cheap loans for small farms to share machines, and lower taxes for farm shops. Not handouts to people, help to businesses that employ people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the village. Our shop is where old Mr Dawson comes every Tuesday just to talk to someone. If small farms go, those places go, and nobody's counting that in any of these pictures.

headlineQuote: People don't drive twenty minutes for sausages. They drive for Ruth behind the counter. A robot can do the counter, but it can't be her.
portrait: Priya Novak is a 27-year-old newcomer on her partner Sam's family's mixed farm, splitting her days between feeding stock, learning lambing and running the farm shop's online orders with AI tools she uses every day. She and Sam live in a caravan behind the barn on about a month's savings, and plan to marry in the village church next summer. Through the scenarios she thinks like a shopkeeper, worrying about office-worker customers and adding cheaper boxes, premium hampers and farm stays. With robots she privately wants one for the lambing shed but fears big farms will win, and she admits that as a newcomer she may be the most replaceable unless she's the one who makes the machines work.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because big farms would get robots first and undercut small family farms unless they stick together.
whatWouldHelp: Grants or cheap loans for small farms to share machines, and lower taxes for farm shops, rather than handouts to individuals.
